A Containerlab lab is one YAML file, called the topology file. It lists the nodes, says what each one runs, and
describes the cables between them. Containerlab reads it and builds the whole lab with one command.

In this part you build a small routed network: two Cisco XRd routers with a Linux host on each side. Then you
verify that the hosts can reach each other through both routers. It assumes you finished
[Part 1](../01-install-containerlab/) and [Part 2](../02-load-images/), and have the XRd and Alpine images.

## The lab you will build

```
  h1 ─────────── xrd1 ─────────── xrd2 ─────────── h2
     192.168.1.0/24    10.0.12.0/30    192.168.2.0/24
```

| Node | Kind | Management address | Data addresses |
|---|---|---|---|
| xrd1 | Cisco XRd router | 172.20.20.11 | 192.168.1.1 (to h1), 10.0.12.1 (to xrd2) |
| xrd2 | Cisco XRd router | 172.20.20.12 | 10.0.12.2 (to xrd1), 192.168.2.1 (to h2) |
| h1 | Alpine Linux host | 172.20.20.21 | 192.168.1.10, gateway 192.168.1.1 |
| h2 | Alpine Linux host | 172.20.20.22 | 192.168.2.10, gateway 192.168.2.1 |

Each router has a static route to the far host network, so traffic from h1 to h2 crosses xrd1 and xrd2.

## The parts of a topology file

```yaml
name: routed            # lab name: used in container names and the lab folder

mgmt:                   # optional: the management network (default shown below)
  network: clab
  ipv4-subnet: 172.20.20.0/24

topology:
  defaults: {}          # optional: settings for every node
  kinds: {}             # optional: settings for every node of a kind
  groups: {}            # optional: named sets of settings that nodes can use
  nodes: {}             # the nodes
  links: []             # the cables between them
```

| Key | Required | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | Yes | Names the lab. Containers are called `clab-<name>-<node>`, and generated files go in a folder `clab-<name>`. Keep it short: it is part of every container name |
| `prefix` | No | Changes the `clab` part of container names; `""` uses bare node names |
| `mgmt` | No | Sets the management network. Leave it out to use the default `clab` network, 172.20.20.0/24 |
| `topology.nodes` | Yes | One entry per node |
| `topology.links` | No | One entry per cable |
| `topology.kinds`, `defaults`, `groups` | No | Shared settings, so you do not repeat yourself |

## The lab's topology file

This is `routed.clab.yml` from the workshop repository:

```yaml
name: routed

topology:
  # Settings shared by every node of a kind.
  kinds:
    cisco_xrd:
      image: ios-xr/xrd-control-plane:7.11.2
    linux:
      image: alpine:3

  nodes:
    xrd1:
      kind: cisco_xrd
      mgmt-ipv4: 172.20.20.11
      startup-config: configs/xrd1.cfg
    xrd2:
      kind: cisco_xrd
      mgmt-ipv4: 172.20.20.12
      startup-config: configs/xrd2.cfg

    h1:
      kind: linux
      mgmt-ipv4: 172.20.20.21
      exec:
        - ip addr add 192.168.1.10/24 dev eth1
        - ip route add 192.168.2.0/24 via 192.168.1.1
    h2:
      kind: linux
      mgmt-ipv4: 172.20.20.22
      exec:
        - ip addr add 192.168.2.10/24 dev eth1
        - ip route add 192.168.1.0/24 via 192.168.2.1

  links:
    # Gi0-0-0-0 here is GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0 inside the router.
    - endpoints: ["h1:eth1", "xrd1:Gi0-0-0-0"]
    - endpoints: ["xrd1:Gi0-0-0-1", "xrd2:Gi0-0-0-1"]
    - endpoints: ["xrd2:Gi0-0-0-0", "h2:eth1"]
```

Open it in the [topology viewer](https://graphs.dynanet.dev/topology?example=routed) to see the lab drawn, with each node's kind, image
and management address when you hover over it. Paste your own topology files there as you write them: it applies
`kinds`, `defaults` and `groups`, and flags links to nodes you have not defined.

You can also work the other way round: in the [topology designer](https://graphs.dynanet.dev/designer), draw the
nodes and links, and it writes the topology file for you, with interface names filled in for each kind. Choose
**Start from… → Routed lab (Part 3)** to open this lab there, or press **Edit in designer** in the viewer. It is a
quick way to sketch a new lab; this part explains what each line of the file it produces means.

### Kinds

`kinds` sets the image once for each kind of node, so the nodes only say which kind they are. To move every router
to a new IOS XR release, you change one line.

### Nodes

Each node needs a `kind`. The other settings used here:

| Setting | Used for |
|---|---|
| `kind` | What the node is: `cisco_xrd`, `arista_ceos`, `linux` and so on. It decides interface names, login and how configuration is applied |
| `image` | The Docker image (here inherited from `kinds`) |
| `mgmt-ipv4` | A fixed management address, so it is the same every time you deploy |
| `startup-config` | A configuration file the node loads at boot. The path is relative to the topology file |
| `exec` | Commands run inside the container once it has started; handy for Linux hosts |

Other settings you will meet:

| Setting | Used for |
|---|---|
| `type` | A model within a kind, for kinds that offer several, such as a chassis type |
| `binds` | Mount files or folders from the host into the node, as `host-path:container-path` |
| `ports` | Publish a node's port on the host, as in `docker run -p` |
| `env` | Environment variables for the node |
| `startup-delay` | Wait this many seconds before starting the node; useful for big labs of heavy nodes |
| `group` | Take settings from a named entry in `topology.groups` |

When a setting appears at several levels, the most specific wins: **node**, then **group**, then **kind**, then
**defaults**.

### The startup configurations

`configs/xrd1.cfg` is the IOS XR configuration that xrd1 loads when it starts:

```
hostname xrd1
username clab
 group root-lr
 group cisco-support
 secret clab@123
!
line default
 transport input ssh
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0
 description to h1
 ipv4 address 192.168.1.1 255.255.255.0
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/1
 description to xrd2
 ipv4 address 10.0.12.1 255.255.255.252
!
router static
 address-family ipv4 unicast
  192.168.2.0/24 10.0.12.2
  0.0.0.0/0 MgmtEth0/RP0/CPU0/0 {{ .MgmtIPv4Gateway }}
 !
!
ssh server v2
end
```

| Lines | What they do |
|---|---|
| `username`, `line default` and `ssh server v2` | The login and the SSH server, as in Part 2 |
| The two `interface` blocks | The addresses towards h1 and towards xrd2 |
| `192.168.2.0/24 10.0.12.2` | The static route to h2's network, through xrd2 |
| `0.0.0.0/0 MgmtEth0/RP0/CPU0/0 {{ .MgmtIPv4Gateway }}` | A default route out of the management interface, so that machines other than the lab host can reach the router (Part 4) |

Containerlab treats a startup config as a template. Before the router starts, it replaces `{{ .MgmtIPv4Gateway }}`
with the gateway address of the management network, which is 172.20.20.1 unless you change the network. The
management interface itself needs no configuration: XRd takes its address from the container.

`configs/xrd2.cfg` is the mirror image: its own addresses, and a route to 192.168.1.0/24 through 10.0.12.1.

### Links

Each link is one cable, written as two `node:interface` endpoints. Use the interface names of each node's kind:
`ethN` for Linux and `Gi0-0-0-N` for XRd. On a Linux node `eth0` is always the management interface, so data links
start at `eth1`. On XRd the management interface is separate, and data links start at `Gi0-0-0-0`.

A link can also connect a node to the host itself, which is useful for reaching a lab from outside:

```yaml
  links:
    - type: host
      endpoint:
        node: xrd1
        interface: Gi0-0-0-2
      host-interface: xrd1-host
```

### Management network

Every node gets a management interface on a Docker network called `clab`, 172.20.20.0/24 by default, and an entry in
the host's `/etc/hosts`. That is how you reach a node by name, for example `ssh clab@clab-routed-xrd1`.

If you give one node a fixed `mgmt-ipv4`, give every node one, so that Docker never hands out an address you have
reserved. To use a different range, add an `mgmt` block:

```yaml
mgmt:
  network: lab-mgmt
  ipv4-subnet: 172.30.30.0/24
```

### Variables

A topology file can read environment variables. This is a simple way to let everyone in a workshop run the same
image version:

```yaml
  kinds:
    cisco_xrd:
      image: ios-xr/xrd-control-plane:${XRD_VERSION:=7.11.2}
```

Plain `containerlab deploy -t routed.clab.yml` then uses version 7.11.2, and
`XRD_VERSION=24.4.2 containerlab deploy -t routed.clab.yml` uses the 24.4.2 image instead, if you have loaded one
with that tag.

## Deploy

First update your copy of the workshop files, then deploy:

```bash
cd ~/dynanet-dev && git pull
cd ~/dynanet-dev/clab-workshop/labs/03-topology
containerlab deploy -t routed.clab.yml
```

The command finishes in a few seconds. It ends with a table of the four nodes, all `running`, with the management
addresses from the file. The routers then need about another minute to start IOS XR and load their configurations.

Containerlab also creates:

| What | Where |
|---|---|
| The lab folder: node configs, an Ansible inventory, a Nornir inventory and `topology-data.json` | `clab-routed/` next to the topology file |
| Host names for the nodes | a `CLAB-routed` block in `/etc/hosts` |
| SSH settings for the nodes | `/etc/ssh/ssh_config.d/clab-routed.conf` |

The lab folder also holds each XRd router's own storage (`clab-routed/xrd1/` and `clab-routed/xrd2/`), which is owned
by root.

## Verify

Run each check. The routers keep starting for about a minute after the deploy finishes, so if a check fails at
first, wait 30 seconds and try again.

| Step | Command | You should see |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Nodes running | `containerlab inspect -t routed.clab.yml` | `xrd1`, `xrd2`, `h1` and `h2` all `running`, with addresses 172.20.20.11, .12, .21 and .22 |
| 2. Router links up | on xrd1: `show ipv4 interface brief` | `GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0` and `GigabitEthernet0/0/0/1` both `Up` and `Up` |
| 3. Static route | on xrd1: `show route static` | `S    192.168.2.0/24 [1/0] via 10.0.12.2` |
| 4. Host to host | `docker exec clab-routed-h1 ping -c 3 192.168.2.10` | `3 packets transmitted, 3 packets received, 0% packet loss` |
| 5. Path | `docker exec clab-routed-h1 traceroute -n 192.168.2.10` | three hops: `192.168.1.1`, `10.0.12.2`, `192.168.2.10` |

For steps 2 and 3, log in with `ssh clab@clab-routed-xrd1` (password `clab@123`), and leave with `exit`.

Or run all the checks at once from the lab folder:

```bash
./verify.sh
```

```
Checking lab routed
  PASS  xrd1 is running with management address 172.20.20.11
  PASS  xrd2 is running with management address 172.20.20.12
  PASS  h1 is running with management address 172.20.20.21
  PASS  h2 is running with management address 172.20.20.22
  PASS  xrd1 GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0 is up
  PASS  xrd1 GigabitEthernet0/0/0/1 is up
  PASS  xrd2 GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0 is up
  PASS  xrd2 GigabitEthernet0/0/0/1 is up
  PASS  xrd1 has the static route to 192.168.2.0/24 installed
  PASS  xrd2 has the static route to 192.168.1.0/24 installed
  PASS  h1 pings h2 (192.168.1.10 -> 192.168.2.10), 0% loss
  PASS  h1 to h2 path is xrd1 -> xrd2 -> h2 (192.168.1.1 10.0.12.2 192.168.2.10)

All checks passed.
```

The script waits for the routers to finish starting before it checks them. Any `FAIL` line says what is wrong.

## Change the lab

| Task | Command |
|---|---|
| Rebuild from scratch after editing the file or a startup config | `containerlab deploy -t routed.clab.yml --reconfigure` |
| Save a router's running config to a file | `docker exec clab-routed-xrd1 /pkg/bin/xr_cli "show running-config" > xrd1-running.cfg` |
| Draw the topology in your browser | Paste the file into the [topology viewer](https://graphs.dynanet.dev/topology) |
| Draw a new or changed lab and get its topology file | Use the [topology designer](https://graphs.dynanet.dev/designer), then **Download .clab.yml** |
| Draw the topology as a Mermaid diagram | `containerlab graph -t routed.clab.yml --mermaid` (writes `clab-routed/graph/routed.clab.mermaid`) |
| Show the lab in a browser | `containerlab graph -t routed.clab.yml`, then open port 50080 on the host |

Without `--reconfigure`, a redeploy reuses the router storage already in the lab folder, so edits to a startup config
do not take effect. `containerlab save` does not work with this lab: for XRd it needs NETCONF, which these
configurations do not turn on.

## Remove the lab

```bash
containerlab destroy -t routed.clab.yml --cleanup
```

`--cleanup` also removes the lab folder `clab-routed`, so the next deploy starts fresh.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Fix |
|---|---|
| Deploy stops with a YAML parsing error | An indentation or quoting mistake. YAML uses spaces, never tabs; align each level by two spaces |
| A node fails with an interface name error | The interface name does not match the node's kind, for example `eth1` on an XRd node instead of `Gi0-0-0-0` |
| Deploy fails because a management address is already taken | Another container already has that `mgmt-ipv4`. Pick a free address or remove the other lab |
| Deploy fails, or nodes are unreachable, because 172.20.20.0/24 is already used on your network | Add an `mgmt` block with a free range (see Management network above) and change every `mgmt-ipv4` to match |
| A startup config change has no effect | Deploy with `--reconfigure` |
| Hosts cannot ping each other but all links are up | Check the static routes (step 3) and the host routes: `docker exec clab-routed-h1 ip route` |
